what: Abercrombie & Fitch sells clothing. It operates two very different brands: Abercrombie, aimed at customers in their twenties and thirties, and Hollister, aimed at teenagers. Both sell through their own stores and online in North America, Europe and Asia.
customers: Younger clothing shoppers, with Abercrombie now serving an older and higher-spending customer than it did historically, and Hollister serving teenagers.
money: Abercrombie & Fitch and Abercrombie Kids, the brand whose repositioning drove the recovery.
Hollister and Gilly Hicks, aimed at teenagers.
moat: Apparel retail has no structural moat, so what matters is execution: reading the customer correctly, buying inventory accordingly and avoiding the markdowns that destroy margin. Abercrombie’s management has done that unusually well, repositioning a brand that was written off as dated into one that an older, higher-spending customer buys at full price — which is genuinely rare in this industry.
risks: Fashion is cyclical in a way that has nothing to do with the economy: a brand that reads its customer correctly for several years can lose them in two seasons, and this company’s own history proves it.
The recovery has already happened. Revenue went from $3.7B to $5.3B and the share price reflects it, so the easy part of the repositioning is behind rather than ahead.
Tariffs on clothing imported from Asia raise landed cost directly, and apparel margins are thin enough for that to matter.
Hollister serves teenagers, the most fickle customer segment there is, and it is nearly half the business.
Eleven analysts average a $170.64 target, about 24% above the current price.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 11.8 times earnings, 1.1 times sales and 7.1 times EV/EBITDA — modest multiples for a business with this margin and growth record.
Free cash flow of $566.5M against a $5.8B market value is a strong yield, funding substantial buybacks.
Cash of $784.6M against $1.2B of debt, much of it leases, is a comfortable position for an apparel retailer.
Selling at full price rather than through discounting is what produced the margin recovery, and it is the hardest thing to achieve in apparel.
International markets are still small relative to North America, which leaves room to grow without needing to win more domestic share.
watch: Full-price selling versus markdowns, and comparable sales at each brand separately. Apparel margins are made or lost on discounting, and the two brands serve different customers who can move in opposite directions.
view: Abercrombie is a genuinely impressive turnaround and that is exactly why it needs to be approached carefully. A brand that was a punchline a decade ago now sells at full price to an older, higher-spending customer, revenue has gone from $3.7 billion to $5.3 billion, and margins expanded while it happened. That is not luck; it is several consecutive years of reading a customer correctly and buying inventory to match. In apparel, that skill is the entire business, and this management team has demonstrated it.

The difficulty is that the market now knows. The turnaround is in the share price, which means you are no longer buying a cheap broken retailer — you are buying a well-run one at 11.8 times earnings and asking whether the execution continues. And here is the uncomfortable fact about apparel: nobody sustains this indefinitely. Fashion cycles turn for reasons that have nothing to do with the economy or management quality, and the clearest evidence is Abercrombie’s own history, where a dominant brand became irrelevant in a few seasons.

The structure of the company makes this sharper than people notice. Hollister is nearly half the business and serves teenagers, who are the most fickle customer segment in retail. Abercrombie serves an older customer who is more stable. Those two halves can and do move in opposite directions, and a blended comparable sales number hides it. Anyone following this should look at them separately — a strong quarter at one brand papering over weakness at the other is exactly the pattern that precedes a reversal.

At 11.8 times earnings, 7.1 times EV/EBITDA and with $566 million of free cash flow funding buybacks, the price is not demanding and the market is clearly discounting the risk of a fashion turn. That seems about right to me: this is a cheap stock because apparel deserves a low multiple, not because anyone misunderstands the company. The thing to watch is the markdown rate. Full-price selling is what produced the margin, and the first sign that the customer has moved on is always discounting, long before it shows up in revenue.
bull: Both brands keep reading their customers correctly, full-price selling holds the margin, and international expansion adds growth to an 11.8 times earnings multiple with heavy buybacks.
bear: The fashion cycle turns at Hollister or Abercrombie, markdowns return, and the margin expansion that drove the whole re-rating unwinds in two seasons.
